title: Kalki
description: Tenth and final avatar of Hindu deity Vishnu
wiki_lead:
Kalki (Sanskrit: कल्कि), also called Kalkin, is the prophesied tenth and final incarnation of the Hindu god Vishnu. According to Vaishnava cosmology, Kalki is destined to appear at the end of the Kali Yuga, the last of the four ages in the cycle of existence (Krita). His arrival will mark the end of the Kali Yuga and herald the beginning of the Satya Yuga, the most virtuous age, before the ultimate dissolution of the universe (Mahapralaya).
In the Puranas, Kalki is depicted as the avatar who will rejuvenate existence by ending the darkest period of adharma (unrighteousness) and restoring dharma (righteousness). He is described as riding a white horse named Devadatta and wielding a fiery sword. The portrayal of Kalki varies across different Puranas, and his narrative is also found in other traditions, including the Kalachakra-Tantra of Tibetan Buddhism and Sikh texts.

In the Puranas, Kalki is depicted as the avatar who will rejuvenate existence by ending the darkest period of adharma (unrighteousness) and restoring dharma (righteousness). Etymology
The name Kalki is derived from Kal, which means "time" (Kali Yuga). The original term may have been Karki (white, from the horse) which morphed into Kalki. This proposal is supported by two versions of Mahabharata manuscripts (e.g. the G3.6 manuscript) that have been found, where the Sanskrit verses name the incarnation to be Karki.


Description


Hindu texts

Kalki is an avatara of Vishnu. Avatar means "descent", and refers to a descent of the divine into the material realm of human existence. Kalki appears for the first time in the Mahabharata.
The Garuda Purana lists ten incarnations, with Kalki being the final one. He is described as the incarnation who appears at the end of the Kali Yuga. He ends the darkest, degenerating, and chaotic stage of the Kali Yuga to remove adharma and ushers in the Satya Yuga, while riding a white horse with a fiery sword. He restarts a new cycle of time. He is described as a Brahmin warrior in the Puranas. It is mentioned in the Puranas that the immortal Chiranjivis will assist him in various stages of his life.
A minor text named Kalki Purana is a relatively recent text, likely composed in Bengal. Its dating floruit is the 18th-century. Wendy Doniger dates the Kalki Purana to between 1500 and 1700 CE.
In the Kalki Purana, Kalki is born into the family of Vishnuyashas and Sumati, in a village called Shambala, on the thirteenth day during the fortnight of the waxing moon. At a young age, he is taught the holy scriptures on topics such as dharma, karma, artha, jñāna, and undertakes military training under the care of the Parashurama (the sixth incarnation of Vishnu). Soon, Kalki worships Shiva, who gets pleased by the devotion and provides him in return a divine white horse named Devadatta (a manifestation of Garuda), a powerful sword, whereby its handle is bedecked with jewels, and a parrot named Shuka, who is an all-knower; the past, the present and the future. Other accessories are also given by other devas, devis, saints, and righteous kings. He fights an evil army and in many wars, ending evil, but does not end existence. Kalki return
grok_lead: In Hindu tradition, Kalki is the tenth and final avatar of the god Vishnu, prophesied to incarnate at the close of the Kali Yuga âthe current age of moral and spiritual declineâto eradicate unrighteousness, vanquish evildoers, and reestablish dharma, thereby initiating a new cycle of the Satya Yuga, the age of truth and purity. This eschatological figure embodies the cyclical renewal inherent in Hindu cosmology, where divine intervention restores cosmic order after periods of chaos and adharma. According to the Vishnu Purana, Kalki will be born as the son of Vishnuyashas, a virtuous Brahman, in the village of Shambhala, endowed with the eight superhuman faculties (ashta-siddhis) that mark Vishnu's divine manifestations. He is depicted as a warrior of unparalleled might, who will "destroy all the mlecchhas [barbarians] and thieves, and all whose minds are devoted to iniquity," using his irresistible power to cleanse the earth of corruption. The Bhagavata Purana elaborates on his iconic appearance: mounted on a swift white horse named Devadatta, Kalki will traverse the world sword in hand, radiating eight mystic opulences and divine qualities, swiftly slaying millions of false kings and thieves who masquerade as rulers. Kalki's advent signals the culmination of the Kali Yuga, described in the Vishnu Purana as lasting 360,000 human years, during which societal virtues erode, leading to widespread violence, deceit, and the dominance of unqualified leaders. His mission extends beyond destruction to renewal: after subduing evil, he will awaken the pure consciousness of survivors, making their minds "as pellucid as crystal," and restore righteousness universally. This prophecy appears across multiple Puranic texts, including the Garuda Purana and Agni Purana, underscoring Kalki's role as the ultimate restorer in the dashavatara (ten avatars) sequence, following predecessors like Rama and Krishna. The symbolism of Kalkiâoften portrayed in art as a resplendent figure on a winged steed wielding a flaming sword ârepresents hope amid degeneration, emphasizing themes of justice, transformation, and the eternal triumph of dharma over adharma in Hindu philosophy. While the exact timing remains prophetic and tied to astronomical alignments, such as the conjunction of the sun, moon, Tishya nakshatra, and Jupiter, Kalki's narrative continues to inspire devotional literature, festivals like Kalki Jayanti, and interpretations in modern Hindu thought.
